# Acoustic emission source location from P-wave arrival time corrected data and virtual field optimization method
Xueyi Shang <sup>a,*</sup>, Yi Wang <sup>b,*</sup>, Runxue Miao
<sup>a</sup> State Key Laboratory of Coal Mine Disaster Dynamics and Control, School of Resource and Safety Engineering, Chongqing University, Chongqing 400044, China
<sup>b</sup> State Key Laboratory of Geodesy and Earth’s Dynamics, Innovation Academy for Precision Measurement Science and Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Wuhan 430077, China
## A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Acoustic emission (AE) Source location P-wave arrival time system error Bayesian inversion Virtual field optimization method (VFOM)
## A B S T R A C T

Acoustic emission (AE) event location plays an important role in structural safety assessments. However, accurately locating an AE event is usually difficult, especially for a small structure. Interestingly, a pencil-lead break (PLB) experiment shows that the P-wave arrival time of a sensor is always significantly different (~260 µs) from that of the other sensors. This time difference is much greater than the P-wave travel time in the range of the experimental sample. Therefore, it can be inferred that there is a P-wave arrival time system error (PATSE) for each sensor. The PATSE may be due to a combined result of the sensor site effect and signal transfer delay time from the sensor to the signal storage. To handle this, a Bayesian inversion framework was built to estimate PATSEs. A synthetic test demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed Bayesian method for noisy P-wave arrival time data. Then, Bayesian inversion was applied to 15 PLB events, which confirmed the existence of PATSE in an AE experiment for the first time. The average PATSE reached 1.47 µs without considering the P-wave arrival time significantly different sensor. The average location error of 25 PLB events was 14.30 mm and 6.58 mm for PATSE unremoved and removed data, respectively. To achieve this, a high-precision virtual field optimization location method (VFOM) was used. This demonstrates the necessity of removing the PATSEs. Finally, the AE event location performance for the PATSE unremoved and removed data was compared, where the AE events were obtained from the uniaxial compression of a red sandstone sample. The results indicated that there was a higher location detection success rate for the corrected data. The AE locations based on the corrected data were in a better correlation with the rock sample failure mode than that without correction. Moreover, increase the signal sampling frequency for AE event identification, use a real-time inverted 3D velocity model and update the PATSEs in real time could be used to further improve the AE event location accuracy.
## 1 Introduction

Acoustic emission (AE) monitoring takes advantage of the transient elastic wavefield generated by rapid released energy of the material. Then, the recorded AE signals are then used for further monitoring investigations, such as waveform analysis, AE event location, magnitude calculation, focal mechanism inversion and velocity tomography. AE waveform analysis and event location are two effective ways to study material crack growth. For the AE waveform analysis, Bhuiyan has made a great contribution [1–5]. Their results show a new avenue of using the piezoelectric wafer active sensors (PWAS) transducer, by capturing more frequency information contained in the AE waveform than conventional AE sensors. Moreover, the waveform evolution is highly related to the physica boundary conditions of the cracks, as well as the fatigue crack growth mechanism. This study focused on the AE event location, which can provide good guidance for monitoring structural health and analysing material fracture processes [6]. However, for conventiona location methods, the AE location result distribution may be negatively correlated with the material failure mode [7]. Currently, an AE event location is usually performed based on P-wave travel time and ray tracing-based location methods. These location results are largely dependent on the quality of the P-wave arrival time data and location techniques.

## 1.1 P-wave arrival time determination

The automatic picking of the absolute P-wave arrival time has been widely studied owing to its convenience. Allen [8] proposed the short-term average to long-term average (STA/LTA) method, which considers the instantaneous characteristics of the first P-wave arrival amplitude and frequency content. Sleeman and van Eck [9] assumed that the signals before and after the P-wave arrival time have different statuses. Based on the maximum likelihood derivation, they proposed the autoregressive Akaike information criterion (AR-AIC) picking method. In addition, the Kurtosis method, fractal dimension method and predominant period method have also been proposed for absolute P-wave arrival time picking. These methods take advantage of the take-off amplitude of a single waveform. However, background noise and signal propagation attenuation can affect the take-off amplitude [10].

To handle the above problem, researchers began to determine the P-wave relative delay time by performing cross-correlation on two windowed characteristic waveforms. The cross-correlation method is mainly dependent on the main peaks of the windowed waveforms. Compared with the absolute P-wave arrival time picking methods, cross-correlation picking is less affected by background noise and signal attenuation. Studies have shown the effectiveness of the waveform cross-correlation method in determining the relative delay times of earthquake waveforms [11,12] and microseismic signals [13]

The above P-wave arrival time picking methods treat the time difference between the observed waveforms as the trigger time difference. These picking methods either set the delay time from sensor to signal storage to the same value or neglect this relative delay time difference. However, it can be different because of the following factors: First, the sensor response time can be influenced by the sensor checking level and sensor contacting state with the material [14]. Then, the sensor monitored signal is transmitted to an amplifier, AE data pre-processing and storage equipment. In addition, the system synchronisation time may exhibit a different shift. The delay time difference from sensor to signal storage is marked as the P-wave arrival time system error (PATSE). To the best of our knowledge, PATSE has yet to be examined or estimated in an AE event location study.
## 1.2 AE event location methods

For the ray tracing-based location methods, through totally summed difference between observed and theoretical arrival times is usually adopted to build the objective function for source location. Since P-wave propagates fastest in seismic signal phases, the direct P-wave arrival time has been widely used in locating seismic sources [6,15]. In contrast, S-wave usually has more energy and is less affected by waveform attenuation, which has prompted researchers to locate seismic event using S-wave arrival time. Kuang et al. [16] found that a common location result can be obtained from S-wave arrival times. The location result was enhanced after including the correction incident angle. Gomberg et al. [17] and Engdahl et al. [18] carried out source location based on P- and S-wave arrival time difference, while Zhou et al. [19] established a P–S phase arrival time difference and P-wave arrival time combined location method. In addition, Zhou et al. [20] found that good location results can be obtained, by combining S-wave arrival time with one or multiple Pwave arrival time. The above multiple seismic phase arrival time-based location methods are all conducted in large-scale structures However, there usually equipped with three phases, S-wave, reflected wave and surface wave, for a small-size structure AE event excitation. This will significantly increase the complexity of P-wave coda. Therefore, it had better only use P-wave arrival time data for AE event location has a small-size structure.

Going back to classical location theory by single-phase arrival time. Geiger’s location method [21] is widely used for the determination of seismic locations. It converts the travel time difference equation into a linear equation to calculate the source location. Geiger s location method adopts a one-step gradient descent inversion, which is fast but can be affected by the initial iteration point Some researchers [22,23] have improved the objective functions and solution techniques of Geiger’s method. Another commonly employed travel time difference-based location method is the double-difference location method [24]. This method assumes that the wavefield propagation paths of two adjacent seismic events are similar, which reduces the influence of structural anomalies on the signal travel time. Li et al. [25] introduced a differential azimuth in the double-difference location method and further improved the location determination accuracy. Another study by Li et al. [26] constructed a hyperboloid and exponential attenuation-based objective function for source location (virtual field optimisation method, VFOM), which reduces the effect of large P-wave arriva time picking errors on location precision. They used the Quasi-Newton iteration method for a quick solution, which may sometimes result in an unstable location result. Thurber [23] and Li et al. [27] separately utilized a second-order partial derivative-based Newton method and the Gauss-Newton method for seismic source location. It improved the location stability to a certain extent, but the secondorder Hessian matrix is computationally expensive. To address the above problems, more stable global inversion methods (e.g., the simplex method, grid search-based method, particle swarm optimization (PSO) algorithm, genetic algorithm and simulated annealing algorithm) have been proposed to solve the location objective function. In addition, time reverse imaging methods have also been proposed for source location [28–30], which successfully predicted the crack size and orientation. It provides more information than pure AE source location and plays an important role in structural health monitoring. A review of AE location methods can be found in Kundu [31] and He et al. [32].

## 1.3 Novelties

The above introduction shows that it had better use P-wave arrival time for an AE event location strictly speaking. The observed Pwave arrival time should be the summation of AE event occurrence time, travel time from source location to sensor location and PATSE from sensor to signal storage where the PATSEs can be different between sensors. Furthermore, a multi-scale grid search strategy wil be combined with the VFOM method [26] to thoroughly locate an AE event. A global view of the content and adopted strategy of this study is shown in Fig. 1. The main innovations and contributions of this study are as follows: A distinct PATSE was observed through pencil-lead break (PLB) tests (e.g., Fig. 1a). Then, a Bayesian inversion framework using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling was established to estimate the PATSEs (Fig. 1b). Moreover, a multi-scale grid search and the PATSE-corrected data-based VFOM (MS-VFOM) location method was proposed to locate an AE event (Fig. 1c), which achieved better location results than the conventiona time difference location method. Finally, the MS-VFOM location method was applied to locate the PLB and AE events of the real data. Both location results show that the location results with PATSEs removed are better than those with PATSEs unremoved. The average location error of the PLB events with PATSEs removed is only 6.58 mm. In addition, the AE event distribution based on the PATSE removed data has a good correlation with the finally observed sample failure mode.

The remainder of this paper is arranged as follows: Section 2 constructs the Bayesian inversion framework for PATSE inversion. Travel-time-based location objective functions were also introduced. Then, the feasibility of the Bayesian PATSE inversion and MS-VFOM location is synthetically tested in Section 3. Section 4 calculates the PATSEs using PLB experimental data. Then, the PLB and AE event location results before and after removing the PATSEs were compared. Section 5 discusses the factors influencing the PATSE inversion and AE event location accuracy. The summary and prospects of this study are presented in Section 6.

## 3 Synthetic test
## 3.1 Bayesian inversion of the PATSEs

Referring to the experiment shown in Section 4, the locations of eight sensors and 15 PLB events (Fig. 2) were selected to test the feasibility of the Bayesian framework. In the synthetic test, all the occurrence times $t _ { 0 } ^ { i }$ were set to 0 $\mu { \sf s } ,$ the PATSEs were set to 1 µs and the P-wave velocity was set to 3.6 mm/us. Then, the theoretical travel time $t _ { 0 } ^ { i j }$ can be calculated using the travel distance and P-wave velocity. In addition, a Gaussian distribution error (u = 0 and σ = 1 us) was added to $t _ { 0 } ^ { i j }$ for testing the effect of the P-wave arrival time quality on the inversion results.

The PATSE Bayesian inversion results before and after adding noise are shown in Fig. 3(a) and (b), respectively. The results showed that the PATSEs were perfectly inversed when no noise was added in the travel time. When there was noise in the travel time, the MCMC converged after 500 iterations, which demonstrates the effectiveness of the Bayesian framework in inversing the PATSEs. It should be mentioned that the inversed PATSEs were different from the preset value of 1 µs. Eqs. (1) and (2) show that the PATSE $T _ { j }$ and AE event occurrence time $t _ { 0 } ^ { i }$ were considered as a whole in the inversion; that is, only the relative $T _ { j }$ rather than absolute $T _ { j }$ will be obtained. In fact, only relative $T _ { j }$ and occurrence times $t _ { 0 } ^ { i }$ are required to locate an AE event.
## 3.2 VFOM location performance for synthetic events

For simplicity, the PATSEs were set to the same value (i.e., ignoring the effect of the PATSEs). Two typical source locations (Fig. 2 (b)) were selected to test the VFOM location method. Event 1 with coordinates of (30, 20, 45) mm was located inside the sensor array and had good ray coverage, while Event 2 with coordinates of (50, 10, 10) mm was located on the sample surface and had poor ray coverage. The sensor locations, velocity model and computation method of ${ { t } _ { 0 } ^ { i j } }$ were the same as those described in Section 3.1. P-wave arrival time errors can occur because of the effects of low signal sampling frequency, waveform propagation attenuation and P-wave arrival time picking method. Therefore, Gaussian noise with a mean value of zero and standard deviations of 1 µs and 2 µs were added to each P-wave arrival time to test the noise resistance. Furthermore, AE signals of adjacent events may be misclassified into one event and the P-wave arrival time picking can be unstable [35], which can result in a large P-wave arrival time picking error. Thus, a large noise of 100 µs added to one P-wave arrival time was also tested. For each event test, the noise addition and event location procedures were repeated 500 times.

The location result distributions and error boxplots of the VFOM, DL1 and DL2 methods are shown in Fig. 4. Overall, the location results for AE events distributed within the range of the sensor array (Event 1) were better than those outside the array (Event 2). When there was no large P-wave arrival time picking error, these three location methods achieved good results. The location results of the VFOM and DL2 methods were slightly superior than the DL1 method. When a large picking error exists in the P-wave arrival time data, both the DL1 and DL2 location errors increased, which is similar to the results obtained in previous studies [36,37]. The VFOM location results remained good in the presence of a large picking error. Overall, the VFOM location errors of the 1 us Gaussian noise test were within 5 mm, which can provide a good basis for analysing the fracturing process of a rock sample (sized $5 0 \times 5 0 \times 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 } )$ Comparatively, the overall VFOM location errors of the 2 µs Gaussian noise test reach 15 mm, which makes it difficult to effectively analyse the fracture processes of a small-size rock sample. The above results indicate the importance of an accurate P-wave arrival time picking in locating an AE event in a small-sized sample; thus, a PATSE with an amplitude order of 1 µs may seriously affect the location result. Moreover, the VFOM method can provide a stable location result than the DL1 and DL2 methods.

## 4.2 PATSE inversion based on the PLB events

The PLB experiment showed that the P-wave arrival time corresponding to sensor 8 was always evidently different (about 260 µs) from that of other sensors, a typical waveform example is shown in Fig. 6. The P-wave travel time in such a small-sized sample should be less than 260 µs. This illustrates the existence of a P-wave arrival time system error. Furthermore, it may be inferred that PATSEs also exist among the other sensors.

The Bayesian inversion proposed in Section 2.1, was conducted to estimate the PATSEs. The inversion was performed based on the 15 PLB events shown in Fig. 2(a). PLB events can largely reduce the spatial dimensions of Bayesian inversion and accelerate the convergence speed. Furthermore, the PLB events have accurate locations, which ensures the estimation accuracy of the PATSEs. To accelerate the convergence speed of the MCMC iterations, the initial value of sensor 8 was set at −260 µs, while those of sensors 1–7 were randomly generated around 0 µs, as shown by the black circles in $\mathrm { F i g . } 7 ( \mathbf { a } )$ . In the MCMC iteration, one parameter was updated each time. The update speed followed a Gaussian distribution sampling, which had a mean value of zero and a standard deviation of 0.25.

The PATSEs, log (likelihood) and acceptance ratio in the MCMC iterations are shown in Fig. 7(a) and (c). A scatterplot of the last 20,000 MCMC iterations is shown in Fig. 7(b). There are some variations of the PATSEs in the MCMC iteration, but they are convergent overall. Then, the likelihood value in the post-burn-in period was much larger than its initial value, indicating that the PATSE-removed data can better fit the observed data. Furthermore, there was a low correlation between PATSEs. The PATSEs approximately followed Gaussian distributions (Fig. 7(b)), which confirmed the reliability of the Bayesian inversion. The Bayesian inversion result was based on the mean value of the last 20,000 MCMC iterations. The approximate PATSEs of sensors 1–8 were $1 . 8 6 , - 0 . 9 5 , - 1 . 4 2 , - 0 . 5 9 , 3 . 1 4$ −1.31, −0.40 and −256.90 µs, respectively. PATSE variations were observed among all sensors; in particular, the PATSE difference between sensors 3 and 5 reached 4.66 µs. According to Section 3.2, ignoring this PATSE would distort the AE event location result in a small rock sample.

## 4.3 MS-VFOM location performance for PLB events

In this section, the PATSEs obtained from the 15 PLB events were adopted to test the location performance. Moreover, 10 new PLB events were also included in the location test, which will help demonstrate the applicability of removing PATSEs better. The PLB event at (50, 20, 50) mm was taken as an example to illustrate the MS-VFOM location result before and after removing the PATSEs and the TCF and location results are shown in Fig. 8. The TCF values without removing the PATSEs were more scattered and smaller than those with PATSE removed. The location error decreased from 17.85 to 4.82 mm. Furthermore, the TCF values and location errors of the 25 PLB events based on the PATSE unremoved and removed data are shown in Fig. 9(a) and (b), respectively. The TCF values after removing the PATSEs were larger than those without removing the PATSEs. Correspondingly, the MS-VFOM location results after removing PATSEs were better and the average location error reduced from 14.31 to 6.58 mm. Notably, only 15 PLB events were used in the PATSE inversion, but all 25 PLB events obtained good location results, which verified that the PATSEs obtained through the Bayesian inversion has good applicability.

Furthermore, PLB tests on a glass cylindrical shell structure were also conducted to verify the proposed MS-VFOM method. The experimental setup is shown in Fig. S1. It should be mentioned that the shortest ray path on the cylindrical shell structure follows the method in [38]. The location results of the 22 PLB events are listed in Table S1. It can be seen that the MS-VFOM location error after removing the PATSEs is much more stable than with PATSEs unremoved. The average location error before and after removing the PATSEs separately are 10.41 cm and 3.15 cm, which is larger than that of the red sandstone and may be due to the effects of a heavier signal attenuation for longer travel distance and poor connection between the sensor and non-flat cylindrical shell structure.
## 4.4 AE application

The stress–time curve of the red sandstone uniaxial compression and cumulative number of AE signals of each sensor are shown in Fig. 10. In the initial uniaxial compression stage, there were a few AE signals that were generated from the rock fracture closure. ## 5 Discussions
## 5.1 Improvement of the PATSE inversion

In the most simplified case, a PATSE does not change with time was adopted in the study. However, the PATSE may change with the testing time. If the PATSE was treated as a variable with the time and event locations were treated as unknown parameters in the
X. Shang et al.
Mechanical Systems and Signal Processing 163 (2022) 108129

PATSE inversion, the inversion dimension would sharply increase (dimension curse). Even after treating the event locations as known parameters, there are still more than 10 dimensions (eight PATSEs plus the number $t _ { 0 } ^ { i }$ of PLB events). The commonly used Newton iteration method and quasi-Newton iteration method converge quickly. However, they are highly dependent on the initial value and easily fall into a locally optimum solution, especially for high-dimensional inversions [37]. Therefore, researchers have begun to use global search algorithms, such as genetic algorithm, simulated annealing, PSO and Bayesian inversion. These methods can jump out of local optimum solutions. However, they usually use random searches with low efficiency to obtain an optimum solution. Currently, grid search is considered the most stable global inversion method, but its search speed is quite slow. Wang et al. [13] proposed a multi scale grid search (coarse and fine grids) for inversion, which reduced the computation cost to some extent. Furthermore, research has combined coarse grid search with a genetic algorithm, simulated annealing and Bayesian inversion; the coarse grid search can provide a good initial solution for these global inversion algorithms [41]. In actual experiments or observation data, there may be no PLB events, then the 3D locations, occurrence time of AE events and PATSEs of AE signals are related parameters in the high-dimension inversion. Then, advanced inversion methods (e.g., trans-dimensional Bayesian inversion [33] and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo [42]) can be used for these high-dimensional inversions.
## 5.2 Influencing factors on AE event location accuracy

For an AE experiment on a small rock sample, the most common difficulty is that the AE location results are not consistent with the failure mode of the rock sample. The AE location accuracy is affected by multiple factors. First, the data transmission rate is limited by the AE monitoring system. With a signal sampling frequency of 1 MHz (i.e., 1 µs) and P-wave velocity of 3.6 mm/µs, the accumulation effects of multiple P-wave sampling time errors may lead to a relatively large location error. Therefore, a higher signal sampling frequency is necessary for a small sample test. Then, P-wave arrivals usually have small energy and the noise and propagation attenuation can make the P-wave arrival unclear [10], which can lead to accumulation of errors. Our results showed that the average PATSE (excluding sensor 8) reached 1.47 µs when the sensor 3 was taken as the reference, which is enough to complicate the AE event location results in a small-size rock sample.

Meanwhile, the source location result is closely related to the objective location function. For example, the VFOM method is more stable than the DL1 and DL2 methods (Fig. 4). Notably, the P-wave velocities in the rock compression process are different at various times and locations. Owing to the stress differences and rock fractures, the velocity difference can reach 2,000 m/s [43,44]. In this study, a homogeneous velocity model is adopted to reduce the location accuracy. In a future study, AE tomography can be applied to obtain a real-time heterogeneous distributed 3D velocity model for the rock sample, then 3D velocity model-based location (e.g., 3D ray shooting method [13]) can provide better location results.
## 6 Conclusions

To address the inferior location accuracy of AE events in a small sample, a Bayesian framework was established to invert the PATSEs of AE signals and a multi-scale grid search algorithm was proposed for the VFOM location. The main conclusions are as follows: (1) The existence of PATSE was found through PLB events and calculated using the proposed Bayesian inversion. (2) The average location error of 25 PLB events was 14.30 mm and 6.58 mm, for PATSEs unremoved and removed data, respectively. This has shown the necessity of removing PATSEs. (3) The combination of multi-scale grid search and VFOM location method was applied to an AE event location, which had a better noise resistance to large P-wave arrival time picking errors than the DL1 and DL2 methods. (4) The AE event location results with PATSE removed were in good correlation with the failure mode of the rock sample, which provides a good approach for analysing the failure process of a small sample. Furthermore, improving the signal sampling frequency, developing efficient global inversion algorithms and using a high-resolution 3D velocity model can improve the AE event location accuracy.
